strengths: The proposed PRPO method provides a well-motivated paragraph-level policy optimization framework that decouples intermediate reasoning alignment from the final prediction reward.
Comprehensive curation of the DF-R5 dataset featuring structured, multi-paragraph forensic reasoning across five diverse generative domains.
Strong empirical results demonstrating clear improvements in cross-domain detection generalizability and explanation alignment over standard MLLM and deepfake forensics baselines.
Extensive ablations validating the design choices, including the ConvNeXT backbone, individual reward formulations (VCR and PCR), and computational efficiency.
weaknesses: The visual consistency reward (VCR) relies on heuristic YAKE keyword extraction and global CLIP embeddings, which may miss subtle, localized pixel-level artifacts.
The prediction consistency reward (PCR) depends on handcrafted keyword lexicons and majority voting, potentially failing on nuanced or mixed-evidence cases.
Evaluation and dataset construction are restricted solely to face-centric imagery, leaving general-scene deepfake detection unexplored.

strengths: Addresses an important problem by focusing on both detection accuracy and verifiable reasoning in vision-language deepfake detection.
Proposes a well-motivated paragraph-level policy optimization (PRPO) approach using visual grounding (VCR) and self-consistency (PCR) without requiring manual paragraph-level supervision.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple unseen generative domains, accompanied by thorough ablation studies and human/LLM explanation quality assessments.
weaknesses: The reward mechanisms rely partly on heuristic keyword extraction (YAKE) and predefined lexicons for consistency matching, which may be brittle or restrict flexible language generation.
Test-time optimization imposes considerable computational latency and sampling overhead per image, limiting suitability for real-time applications.
The scope of the benchmark and methodology is predominantly confined to face-centric manipulations, leaving broader scene-level generative forgeries unexamined.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge in media forensics: moving beyond opaque binary classification to produce grounded, multi-paragraph forensic reasoning explaining why an image is authentic or manipulated.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation using a strict leave-one-domain-out generalization protocol across five diverse generative backbones (DDIM, PixArt, SD-2.1, SiT, StyleGAN3), demonstrating competitive F1 gains over both specialized forensic models (e.g., SIDA, UnivCLIP) and general-purpose MLLMs.

Well-structured ablation studies examining the contribution of individual components, including the ConvNeXT backbone vs. ViT, the auxiliary binary loss, individual reward terms (VCR vs. PCR), and comparison against sample-level RL baselines (PPO, GRPO).

Thorough evaluation of explanation quality combining a multi-dimensional LLM-as-a-judge rubric (evaluating accuracy, evidence grounding, reasoning quality, calibration, and clarity) with an expert human evaluation study.
weaknesses: Ambiguity regarding the exact test-time RL protocol: The paper describes PRPO as operating at 'test time' (Section 3.3 and Appendix E.2), but does not fully clarify whether the policy weights are adapted per test instance/batch and discarded, or continuously fine-tuned. Moreover, running multi-sample rollouts, keyword extraction, and policy gradient updates at inference creates substantial computational overhead (7.4–13.8 seconds per iteration across 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs, as reported in Table 20), which may limit real-time applicability.

Heuristic reliance of the Prediction Consistency Reward (PCR): PCR relies on rule-based dictionary matching (lists of fake, real, and negation terms in Algorithm 2) to determine the sentiment of each paragraph. Forensic descriptions often involve nuanced, hedged, or complex syntactic constructions (e.g., 'no obvious signs of unnatural smoothing, yet the hairline displays subtle blending artifacts') that can easily mislead simple keyword-matching heuristics.

Potential semantic shortcut in Visual Consistency Reward (VCR): VCR extracts keywords using YAKE and computes global image-text cosine similarity via the frozen CLIP ConvNeXT encoder. Because CLIP aligns high-level semantic concepts, there is a risk that VCR primarily rewards keywords corresponding to prominent facial attributes (e.g., hair color, gender, accessories) rather than fine-grained, localized forensic artifacts.

Scope limited to face-centric images: The dataset and experiments are exclusively focused on facial deepfakes derived from DF40, leaving the generalizability of the proposed paragraph-level grounding to open-domain or natural-scene synthetic image detection unverified.

strengths: Significance of the task: Combining deepfake detection with grounded, interpretable reasoning is an important and timely problem, as traditional forensic models function largely as black boxes.

Dataset contribution: The creation of the DF-R5 dataset (115k image-reasoning pairs across 5 generative models) provides a structured resource with fine-grained feature categorizations (74 curated forensic features) to support explainable detection.

Granular RL design: Decomposing reasoning traces into paragraph-level features and assigning relative advantages per paragraph is a sensible conceptual extension over token-uniform advantage weighting (e.g., standard GRPO).

Comprehensive empirical benchmarking: The authors evaluate across five diverse generative model families under leave-one-domain-out settings and compare against both specialized forensics detectors and general multimodal LLMs.
weaknesses: Ambiguity regarding 'Test-Time RL' protocol and evaluation setup: The paper repeatedly frames PRPO as a test-time RL algorithm (Abstract, Section 1, Section 3.3). However, the implementation details state that PRPO is optimized using 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs with AdamW and Verl. It is completely unclear whether PRPO is updating weights during inference on unlabelled test images (transductive/test-time adaptation) or if it is an offline post-training RL stage on the training corpus. If it optimizes on test data at test time, the compute cost, latency, and fairness relative to frozen/static baselines must be clearly defined and controlled.

Brittle and heuristic reward functions susceptible to reward hacking: The Prediction Consistency Reward (PCR) relies on rudimentary dictionary matching (Algorithms 1–3) using predefined sets of positive, negative, and negation words. Natural explanatory text frequently includes nuanced concessive structures (e.g., 'While the eye highlights appear slightly irregular, the overall anatomical geometry remains natural'), which such keyword matching misclassifies. RL policies optimized against hardcoded word lists are notoriously prone to exploitation and reward hacking.

Lack of human evaluation or visual grounding verification: The reasoning quality evaluation (Table 6) relies exclusively on zero-shot prompting of GPT-4o. LLM-as-a-judge is known to suffer from stylistic and verbosity biases. Without human expert evaluation or quantitative localization metrics (e.g., bounding-box pointing games or attention map overlap with true manipulated regions), the claim of 'evidence-grounded explanations free of hallucination' is insufficiently substantiated.

Fairness of baseline comparisons: In Table 4, it is unclear whether existing baselines (e.g., FakeShield, UnivCLIP, SIDA) were fine-tuned on the proposed DF-R5 dataset or only evaluated out-of-the-box. If only the proposed method had access to the 115k fine-tuning pairs, the performance gap may stem primarily from supervised domain adaptation rather than the PRPO formulation.

Presentation and writing oversights: The paper leaves an incomplete sentence at the end of the Introduction ('Code and dataset are available at \n 2 RELATED WORK'), and Table 10 inadvertently refers to the method as 'DPRPO (ours)' instead of 'PRPO'.

strengths: Addresses a crucial and timely problem in synthetic media forensics: providing faithful, fine-grained visual reasoning alongside binary real/fake classification.

The DF-R5 data construction pipeline is methodically structured, using multi-model feature discovery to identify 74 forensic-relevant features followed by structured scoring and reasoning consolidation.

The architectural transition to a convolutional visual encoder (CLIP ConvNeXT) in DX-LLaVA is well-motivated for deepfake detection, as CNNs possess inductive biases that better capture high-frequency textural artifacts than standard ViTs.
Empirical cross-domain detection performance across five challenging generative models (DDIM, PixArt, SD-2.1, SiT, StyleGAN3) shows consistent gains over prior multimodal and forensic baselines.
weaknesses: Ambiguity regarding the training setting: The paper repeatedly frames PRPO as a 'test-time reinforcement learning algorithm' (e.g., in the Abstract, Section 1, Section 2, and Section 3.3). However, Section 4.1 describes training on 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs using the verl package with policy gradient updates and KL regularization against a reference policy. It remains unclear whether PRPO is an offline RL fine-tuning stage or true test-time adaptation run dynamically per test image. If it is test-time RL, there is no discussion of computational overhead, inference latency, or optimization steps per test sample.

Heuristic and fragile reward design: Both reward components rely on brittle heuristics. The Prediction Consistency Reward (PCR) relies on superficial dictionary lookups and rule-based negation parsing (Algorithms 1–3), which struggle with nuanced or contrastive phrasing (e.g., 'while the lighting appears natural, the hair edges are manipulated'). Meanwhile, the Visual Consistency Reward (VCR) relies on YAKE keyword extraction matched against frozen CLIP image embeddings, which often fail to capture subtle, localized forensic inconsistencies.

Evaluation of reasoning quality is limited to LLM-as-a-judge: Explanation quality (Table 6) is assessed entirely by GPT-4o without human expert evaluation, user studies, or pixel-grounded verification. Automated LLM evaluation is prone to length bias and cannot reliably verify whether subtle forensic artifacts cited by the model are genuinely present in the image.

Missing ablation and computational profiling: The paper does not report the time or memory overhead incurred by YAKE token extraction and CLIP similarity computations during RL rollouts, nor does it explore the sensitivity of the policy to the paragraph-weighting factor or dictionary composition.

strengths: Important and timely research topic: moving multimodal deepfake detection beyond black-box classification toward structured, interpretable forensic reasoning.
Construction of DF-R5, a large-scale dataset (115k samples across 5 generative architectures) accompanied by a systematic 74-feature forensic taxonomy covering diverse facial and artifact categories.
Sensible architectural adaptation (DX-LLaVA) that replaces the standard CLIP-ViT encoder with CLIP-ConvNeXT to retain sensitivity to localized, high-frequency generative artifacts.

Extensive cross-generator empirical evaluations across five unseen domains (DDIM, PixArt, SD, SiT, StyleGAN3), demonstrating competitive classification performance against both dedicated detectors and general MLLMs.
weaknesses: Conceptual ambiguity regarding 'Test-Time RL': The manuscript repeatedly labels PRPO as a test-time reinforcement learning algorithm (Abstract, Section 1, Section 3.3, Section 4.5). However, Section 4.1 describes standard distributed training on 8 H200 GPUs using AdamW with learning rate 3e-7 via the verl framework. If PRPO is adapted at test time per test instance/domain, the paper omits critical operational details: number of adaptation steps, compute cost, memory footprint, and latency per sample. If it is trained offline as post-training using label-free rewards, calling it 'test-time RL' is a major misnomer.

Heuristic and fragile reward formulations: (i) The Prediction Consistency Reward (PCR) relies on rudimentary dictionary lookups (Algorithms 1–3) with hardcoded keyword lists (F, R, N), which can be easily gamed or fail on paraphrased/complex linguistic syntax. (ii) The Visual Consistency Reward (VCR) uses CLIP cosine similarity over YAKE-extracted keywords; however, CLIP encoders generally prioritize global semantic content over fine-grained forensic artifacts (e.g., subtle pixel blending or pupil deformities), risking rewarding generic image descriptions rather than true forensic grounding.

Lack of grounded or human evaluation for reasoning quality: Explanation faithfulness is evaluated exclusively by prompting GPT-4o (Table 6). Without human expert studies or objective localization metrics (e.g., IoU or pointing games against ground-truth manipulation masks), it remains unverified whether the generated explanations correspond to actual physical manipulation areas or merely articulate plausible-sounding hallucinations.
Presentation and reporting discrepancies: The method is inconsistently named in the tables (e.g., 'DPRPO' in Table 10 vs. 'PRPO' elsewhere), along with typos such as 'classifider' in Section 3.2.
